summary:
Stella Sanitas is an autonomous astronaut health and telemetry system built for deep-space missions, where crews can’t rely on real-time help from Earth. It combines three views in one web app: an astronaut tablet, a flight surgeon console, and a ground telemetry station. It tracks live vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, core temperature, HRV) and maps spaceflight-specific risks such as SANS (optic disc edema), fluid shifts, bone density loss, calf sarcopenia, circadian hormone rhythms, and cosmic radiation exposure. Astronauts complete daily self-evaluations and interactive vision and Amsler grid tests, and AI-assisted decision support suggests differential diagnoses and countermeasures. A latency simulator models communication delays from low Earth orbit to Mars (up to ~21 minutes), with encrypted telemetry queued for Houston.

It addresses the challenge of delivering medical care when Earth can’t respond quickly. This matters because long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars depend on crews monitoring, diagnosing, and managing their own health safely.
details:
What it does and how it works
Stella Sanitas is a web-based health and telemetry system for crews on deep-space missions, where Earth can’t respond in real time. It has three role-based views: an astronaut tablet, a flight surgeon console (Houston/JSC), and a ground telemetry station. The system:

  • Shows live vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, core temperature, HRV) and an ECG-style rhythm readout.
  • Maps spaceflight-specific risks through an interactive physiological system map covering SANS (optic disc edema), cephalad fluid shifts, bone density loss, calf sarcopenia, and renal and hormone changes.
  • Charts bone density decline, OCT retinal thickness, cortisol/melatonin rhythms, and cosmic radiation dosimetry against NASA exposure limits.
  • Lets astronauts log daily self-evaluations and take built-in vision and Amsler grid tests.
  • Lists biomarkers and offers AI-assisted differential diagnoses and countermeasure recommendations.
  • Simulates communication delays from low Earth orbit (0.28 sec) to Mars conjunction (21 min), queuing encrypted telemetry packets for Earth.
  • Registers new crew members and generates a printable medical report.

Benefits

  • Crews can monitor and act on their own health during communication blackouts.
  • Flight surgeons get structured, prioritized data instead of raw streams.
  • Early warning alerts help catch conditions like SANS before they become severe.
  • Delay-aware design means medical data still reaches Earth reliably.

Intended impact
To support safer long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars by shifting medical care from real-time ground control toward autonomous, AI-supported onboard care.

Tools and technologies
The page appears to be a single-page, mobile-friendly web app built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with interactive charts and a responsive tablet layout. It lists AES-256-GCM/CCSDS for encryption and Goldstone DSN for ground links. The page credits “SI (Synthetic Intelligence)” as its author. I could only read the rendered text, so please confirm the exact frameworks, libraries, AI models, and any hardware before submitting.

Creativity
It combines clinical decision support, orbital communication physics, and a mission simulation in one interface. Features like the in-app Amsler grid test, the delay simulator, and the role-switching views make it feel like a working flight system rather than a static dashboard.

Factors considered

  • Communication latency and offline autonomy
  • Data security and encryption
  • Mission-specific health risks (vision, bone, muscle, radiation, circadian disruption)
  • Usability for astronauts under workload, on a tablet
  • Clear alerting and clinical interpretation for flight surgeons
  • Scalability to multiple crew members and mission legs
